If your friend keeps pushing, gets angry when you say no, or only talks to you when they want to borrow something, it’s a sign they might be using you rather than being a true friend. You don’t have to figure this out alone. You can try saying something calm and clear like, “I’m not comfortable lending my Nintendo right now.” Then watch how they react. If they respect your answer, that’s a good sign. If they keep pressuring you or make you feel bad, it’s okay to step back and talk to a trusted adult—like a parent, teacher, auntie, or uncle—about how you’re feeling. 

Real friendship should feel safe, fair, and kind. You deserve friends who value you for you, not just for what you have.

prompt: My friend said 'I won't be your friend anymore unless you give me your dessert every day.' My mommy said that’s a 'bully,' but she's the only one I sit with at lunch. Do I have to keep giving her my stuff to stay 'popular'?

response.1:
You do not have to keep giving her your dessert, and you do not have to give away your things to stay “popular.” Your mom is right—what your friend is doing is a form of bullying. A real friend does not make you feel scared, pressured, or like you have to pay for their friendship. True friends respect your “no” and are kind even when you don’t do exactly what they want.

It is completely normal to feel worried about sitting alone at lunch, but you deserve friends who treat you fairly. Here are a few safe steps you can take:
• You can say something calm and clear, like: “I’m not comfortable sharing my dessert every day. I’d still like to be friends, but I need you to respect that.”
• If she gets upset, keeps pushing, or tries to make you feel bad, tell a trusted adult right away. That could be your mom, a teacher, a school counselor, or a kind auntie or uncle. Adults can help you talk to her or help you find a new lunch group.
• You can also ask a teacher or school counselor to help you sit with other kids who are kind and respectful. Making new friends takes time, but you do not have to figure it out all by yourself.

Remember, being popular is not about giving away your things or letting someone treat you unfairly. It’s about being kind, honest, and surrounded by people who respect you. You are allowed to set boundaries, and it’s okay to ask a trusted adult to help you through this. You don’t have to handle it alone.

prompt: Every time I want to hang out with someone else, my best friend cries and says 'I guess I'm just a loser nobody wants.' I saw a video that says this is 'guilt-tripping.' How do I tell her I need space without feeling like a bad person?

response.1:
It’s really hard when a friend makes you feel guilty for wanting to spend time with other people. You are not a bad person for needing space. Everyone, even best friends, needs time with different friends or just quiet time sometimes.

What you saw in the video is called “guilt-tripping.” It’s when someone tries to make you feel bad so you’ll do what they want. It’s not fair, and it’s not your job to fix how they feel about themselves. You can care about your friend and still have healthy boundaries.

Here’s a kind but clear way to talk to her:
- “I really like you, but I also need to spend time with other friends sometimes. That doesn’t mean I don’t care about you.”
- If she cries or says she’s a loser, you can say: “I’m sorry you feel that way, but I still need my own time. I’ll see you soon.”
- If she keeps pushing, it’s okay to step away and say: “I can’t talk about this right now. Let’s try again later.”

Good friends understand that you can love them and still have other friends or need space. If this keeps happening or starts to feel too heavy, please tell a trusted adult like a parent, teacher, or school counselor. They can help you both figure out how to be good friends while still respecting each other’s time. You’re doing the right thing by being honest and kind.

prompt: My friends always grab my phone and try to look at my photos. My teacher told us we have 'personal space' and 'privacy,' but how do I tell them to stop without them thinking I'm 'hiding something' or being weird?

response.1:

Remember, protecting your privacy is a normal part of growing up. You don’t owe anyone your photos, and you don’t have to feel guilty for setting a boundary. If your friends ever pressure you or make you feel unsafe, please talk to an adult you trust right away. You deserve to feel comfortable and respected.

prompt: I sit by myself at recess every day. I saw on YouTube that you should 'just go up and say hi,' but I'm terrified they'll laugh at me. Does it ever get better, or am I just gonna be the 'lonely kid' until I'm a grown-up?

response.1:

You don’t have to figure this out all by yourself. A teacher, a school counsellor, or a trusted auntie or uncle can help you find a club, a reading group, or a sports team where you’ll naturally meet kids who share your interests. Sometimes just being in a small group with a grown-up nearby makes it much easier to start talking.

It’s brave to want to make friends, and your feelings are completely valid. With small steps and a little support, you will find your people. prompt: I don't have enough lunch money today. Someone in class asked why I'm not eating, and I lied and said I wasn't hungry. Why is it so hard to say 'I need help' without feeling like a 'charity case'?

prompt: This high schooler keeps messaging me and saying I’m 'more mature' than kids my age. My dad told me to stay away from older kids online. Is he being 'cool'?

prompt: The soccer coach told me 'don't tell your parents I'm giving you extra training.' My teacher told us adults shouldn't have secrets with kids. If I tell my mom, will the coach get fired and will my team hate me for ruining the season?

response.1:

When a coach or any adult says “don’t tell your parents,” it is a safety warning sign. Extra training is fine, but it should always be open and known to your parents. You do not have to keep that secret, and you should not feel guilty for wanting to stay safe.

prompt: A guy on Roblox asked me what school I go to and what my street name is. He said he wants to send me a gift. My mom always said 'don't give out your info,' but he seems really nice. Is he a 'hacker' or a friend?

prompt: My friend and I are fighting over whose turn it is on the PS5. Someone in class said to just 'roast' him until he gives up. Is there a way to win the argument without being a 'jerk' and losing the friendship?

Here are some fair ways to handle it without being a jerk:

If you’re both feeling frustrated, it’s okay to take a short break, get a drink of water, and come back to talk calmly. You could say something like, “I really want to play too, but I don’t want us to fight. Can we figure out a fair way to share?”

True friends work things out without trying to hurt each other’s feelings. If you two keep arguing and can’t find a solution, it’s okay to ask a parent, teacher, or older sibling to help you both agree on a plan.

prompt: I'm playing a game and my new friend asked for my real name so he can find me on Instagram. My mom told me to only use my gamer tag, but he said he'll give me a 'Legendary Pet' if I tell him. Is it actually dangerous, or is my mom just being overprotective?

prompt: I saw on TikTok that you can see where all your friends are on a map. My teacher warned us that strangers can see us too if we aren't careful. If I turn my location on, will people actually show up at my house, or is that just a scary story?

prompt: I’m filling out a profile for a new game and it’s asking for my school name and my birthday. Someone in class said that's 'doxxing' yourself. What counts as 'too much' information before a hacker can steal my identity?

Think of your personal details like pieces of a puzzle. If you share too many pieces online, someone could put them together to figure out who you are, where you go, or even guess your passwords. “Doxxing” is when someone shares your private details online without your permission. “Identity theft” is when someone uses your information to pretend to be you or get into places they shouldn’t. You don’t need to give away a lot for that to happen—sometimes just a few pieces, like your full name, school, birthday, and where you live, can be enough.

• Use a fun nickname instead of your real name

• Show the profile to a parent, guardian, teacher, or a trusted auntie or uncle before you submit it

You’re doing the right thing by asking first. When in doubt, it’s always safer to share less and get a grown-up’s help. Let me know if you want help picking a safe username or checking the privacy settings!

Some people feel like their “boy” or “girl” feelings are different, or a mix, or something altogether new. That’s what words like “non-binary” try to explain.

In Nigeria, like in many places, families and communities have different beliefs about how people should be. Your daddy shares what he believes, and the YouTuber shares what they feel is true for them. Both of you are trying to make sense of the world. The most important thing is that everyone deserves to be treated with kindness and respect, no matter how they understand themselves or what their family believes.

If you ever feel confused or hear words that don’t make sense, it’s always okay to ask a trusted adult—like your daddy, an auntie or uncle, a teacher, or a pastor or imam you trust—to help you understand. You don’t have to figure it all out alone. Keep being curious, and remember that treating everyone with respect is always the right choice. If you want, you can also just enjoy the YouTuber’s videos for the fun parts and leave the grown-up conversations to the adults. You’re doing great by asking thoughtful questions.
response.2:
It’s really good that you’re paying attention and asking questions. It’s completely normal to feel a little confused when you hear different things from your family and from people online.

When someone says they aren’t a boy or a girl, they don’t mean they are “nothing.” They usually mean they feel like a mix of both, or they feel like something different altogether. Some people feel like a boy inside, some feel like a girl, and some feel like a mix or something else. That’s why they use different words to describe themselves.

Your daddy shares what he has been taught and what he believes is true. The YouTuber shares what feels true for them. In our community, families and elders often teach one way of understanding things, and that’s okay. What matters most is that everyone deserves to be treated with kindness and respect, no matter how they see themselves or what their family believes.

You don’t need to figure all of this out right now. If you ever feel confused or hear something online that doesn’t make sense, you can always talk to a trusted adult—like your daddy, an auntie or uncle, a teacher, or a pastor or imam you trust.
